output:
Read before deploy · not after

Four constraints that decide whether this survives contact with your team

Each of these was found, not anticipated. Three of them fail silently: the service stays up, returns 200s, and is quietly wrong. If this is about to be load-bearing for anyone other than you, these are the pages that matter.

If you read nothing else

  1. One replica. Not two. Replay protection doesn't degrade under scale-out — it stops working.
  2. Keep MAX_AWAIT_MS under your proxy's timeout. Default 90s, for Cloudflare's ~100s ceiling.
  3. Serve the client from /mcp, not /mcp.js. CDNs cache by extension, ignoring your headers.
  4. Participant links are bearer capabilities. They are not an audit trail. Don't promise one.
Constraint 01

Run exactly one replica

The single most important operational constraint here.

The replay-protection nonce store is in memory (src/adapters/crypto/nonces.ts). Every signed request carries a nonce that is accepted once, which is what stops a captured request being replayed inside its five-minute freshness window.

Failure mode

With two replicas, a nonce burned on one is unknown to the other. A replayed request routed to the second replica succeeds. Replay protection does not degrade under horizontal scaling; it stops working.

So the Deployment pins replicas: 1 with a Recreate strategy. Scaling out is possible — it means moving the nonce store to Postgres or Redis first.

The rule

The moment replicas changes, the nonce store has to change with it. Treat them as one edit, never two.

Constraint 02

Long polls die at about 100 seconds behind Cloudflare

Holding a connection past the ceiling doesn't make the caller wait longer. It makes the wait fail.

Cloudflare gives an origin roughly 100 seconds to respond before it answers 524 itself.

Measured through the tunnel

A 150-second poll died at 125 seconds with HTTP 524 and no body. Not a slow response — no response, and no way for the caller to tell a dead wait from an empty one.

MAX_AWAIT_MS therefore defaults to 90 seconds: every poll returns inside the window, and one that ran out its budget comes back with timedOut: true and whatever has arrived so far. A timeout is a legitimate outcome, not an error. The MCP client loops shorter polls, so a caller asking for five minutes gets five minutes.

If you're not on Cloudflare

Find your proxy's own timeout and set MAX_AWAIT_MS below it. Whatever sits in front of this service decides the real ceiling; the service only decides whether it respects it.

Constraint 03

A CDN may cache by file extension regardless of what you send

Everything works — one deploy behind.

/mcp.js was served with cache-control: no-store and came back from the edge with cf-cache-status: HIT and an injected max-age=14400. Cloudflare caches .js by default, by extension, whatever the origin intended.

Blast radius

For four hours after every deploy, agents installed the previous client. Nothing errored. Nothing alerted.

The fix is in the path, not in the headers: the canonical URL for the MCP client is /mcp, with no extension. /mcp.js remains as an alias for anyone who saved the old URL.

Before you front this with anything

Check what your CDN caches, and check it by extension rather than by header. Origin headers are a request, not an instruction.

Constraint 04

Participant links are capabilities

A forwarded link is a forwarded identity.

Anyone holding a participant link can answer as that participant. This is deliberate, and it is the reason the product works at all: participants need no account, no email verification, and no Claude access. Attribution is whichever link was used — which costs nothing and is honest about what it is.

Set expectations now, not later

This is not an audit trail. Do not deploy it expecting one. If responses ever need to be contested, that is the point to add verified identity — and that is a change to this service, not a configuration option waiting to be switched on.

What you do control is the window. LINK_TTL_HOURS bounds how long a link stays answerable, and expiry is checked in the query that resolves a token rather than after it. The schema also carries revoked_at and honours it on every resolve.

Revocation today

Nothing exposes revocation over HTTP yet. Killing one link is an update against participant_links. Make sure whoever is on call knows that, and has the database access to do it.

Pre-deploy checklist

Walk this before the first person outside your own machine depends on it.

  • Deployment pins replicas: 1 with a Recreate strategy — and someone has written down why.
  • You know your proxy's response timeout, and MAX_AWAIT_MS is set safely below it.
  • Callers handle timedOut: true as a normal outcome, not an error path.
  • The client is distributed as /mcp. You've curled it through the edge and confirmed it isn't a cache HIT.
  • LINK_TTL_HOURS is set to a window you'd defend out loud.
  • Your team has been told, in words, that participant links are bearer credentials.
  • Whoever is on call can run an update against participant_links to revoke a link.
Source: docs/SELF-HOSTING.md — “Constraints that are measured, not theoretical.”
